title: The rich young man (Mark 10:17–22)
hookLine: Jesus looked at him and loved him, then asked for everything

cards: A man comes running up as Jesus sets out on the road again. He kneels in the road and asks a question as big as they come: "Good Master, what shall I do that I may inherit eternal life?"
Jesus pushes back on the compliment first: why call me good? No one is good but God alone. Then: you know the commandments.

Don't commit adultery, don't kill, don't steal, don't bear false witness, don't defraud, honor your father and mother. And the man says, I've kept all these since I was young. Nothing in Mark suggests he's boasting.

teach.h: HE LOOKED, AND LOVED, AND ASKED.
teach.b: In the King James Bible: "Then Jesus beholding him loved him, and said unto him, One thing thou lackest: go thy way, sell whatsoever thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come, take up the cross, and follow me."
Look at the order. He looks at him. He loves him.
Only then does he ask the hardest thing.

teach.h: ONLY MARK SAYS HE LOVED HIM.
teach.b: Mark is the only gospel that says Jesus loved him; Matthew and Luke tell the story and leave it out. And Mark never says he was young. Matthew calls him a young man, and Luke calls him a ruler.
Our title stitches the Gospels together.
Then the line that closes the scene: "And he was sad at that saying, and went away grieved: for he had great possessions." He doesn't argue or sneer. He just can't do it, and walks away sad.
And Jesus lets him go. What happened to him after? The Gospels are silent.
Christians read the command in more than one way. Some have taken it literally: the early monk Anthony of Egypt, the story goes, heard this read in church and gave away his family's land.

teach.h: LITERAL, OR AIMED AT HIS HEART?
teach.b: Others read it as aimed at this one man, and at whatever holds a person back from following.
Either way, Mark puts the love first: the hard word comes after the long look, from someone who, the text says, loved him.

how: Some Christians, especially in monastic orders, take vows of poverty inspired by this story; others read it as a call to examine what holds them back, and to give generously to the poor.

o: to love, to care deeply for someone
to work hard for a fair wage
to admire someone for their goodness

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: took it literally, the story goes

s: Mark calls him a young man
Mark never says young. Matthew says young; Luke says ruler.
only Mark says Jesus loved him
"Jesus beholding him loved him." Matthew and Luke leave it out.
he went away sad and grieved, because he had great possessions.

games.q: you're the man. you've kept every commandment since youth. Jesus looks at you with love and says: sell everything, give it to the poor, and follow me. what do you do?
games.why: "he was sad at that saying, and went away grieved: for he had great possessions." and Jesus let him go, still loved.

practice: Think of someone you'd like to tell something to, advice, a correction, a hard truth, and before any of that, just look at them in your mind: their face, what they're carrying, what they're good at.
Stay there a moment, and let some warmth toward them come, if it will; if you pray, ask to see them the way Jesus looked at the man. Only then, if you still need to, decide what you'd say.

wordCard.voice: Agapao, the Greek verb for loved. A good man who ran to Jesus, was loved, was asked for everything, and walked away sad.

orig.note: Greek: he loved, from agapaō. Mark 10:21: Jesus looked at him and loved him.

carryVoice: Your line: he loved him. He let the man walk away, still loved. That's day two hundred two.
